title.zh: 卷75 列傳第40 儒林
title.raw: 卷75 列傳第40 儒林 Volume 75 Biographies 40: Confucian Scholars

sentences.zh: 儒林儒之為教大矣，其利物博矣。

translations.literal: [Confucian Scholars.] The teaching of Confucianism is vast; the benefit it confers upon all things is broad.
translations.idiomatic: Confucian Scholars. The teaching of the Confucian school is vast in scope, and the good it does for the world is far-reaching.

sentences.zh: 篤父子，正君臣，尚忠節，重仁義，貴廉讓，賤貪鄙，開政化之本源，鑿生民之耳目，百王損益，一以貫之。

translations.literal: It deepens father and son, rectifies ruler and minister, esteems loyalty and integrity, values benevolence and righteousness, prizes integrity and yielding, despises greed and baseness, opens the source of government and transformation, carves open the ears and eyes of the living people, and through the additions and subtractions of a hundred kings, threads it all as one.
translations.idiomatic: It strengthens the bond between father and son, sets ruler and minister in their proper roles, exalts loyalty and integrity, upholds benevolence and righteousness, honors integrity and modesty, and disdains greed and vulgarity. It opens the wellsprings of government and moral transformation and awakens the eyes and ears of the common people; through generations of kings who added to or trimmed away its doctrines, one unbroken thread runs throughout.

sentences.zh: 雖世或汙隆，而斯文不墜，經邦致治，非一時也。

translations.literal: Although the age may rise or fall in fortune, this culture does not perish; governing the state and bringing order is not the work of a single moment.
translations.idiomatic: Though fortunes of the age may wax and wane, this literary tradition does not perish; ordering the realm and achieving good government is never the achievement of a single age alone.

sentences.zh: 涉其流者，無祿而富，懷其道者，無位而尊。

translations.literal: Those who enter its current are rich without salary; those who embrace its Way are honored without office.
translations.idiomatic: Those who enter its stream grow wealthy though they hold no stipend; those who cherish its Way stand honored though they hold no rank.

sentences.zh: 故仲尼頓挫于魯君，孟軻抑揚于齊後，荀卿見珍于強楚，叔孫取貴于隆漢。

translations.literal: Therefore Confucius was thwarted by the ruler of Lu, Mencius was held back and advanced by the queen of Qi, Xunzi was treasured in powerful Chu, and Gongsun Hong won esteem in flourishing Han.
translations.idiomatic: Thus Confucius met setbacks under the ruler of Lu, Mencius was alternately restrained and promoted under the queen mother of Qi, Xun Qing was prized in powerful Chu, and Gongsun Hong won honor in the flourishing Han.

sentences.zh: 其餘處環堵以驕富貴，安陋巷而輕王公者，可勝數哉！

translations.literal: As for the rest who dwelt in a ring of walls yet looked down on wealth and rank, or were content in mean alleys yet held kings and dukes lightly—can they be counted?
translations.idiomatic: As for the countless others who lived in a bare room yet looked down on wealth and rank, or were content in humble lanes yet held kings and dukes lightly—who could number them all?

sentences.zh: 自晉室分崩，中原喪亂，五胡交爭，經籍道盡。

translations.literal: From the time the Jin house split apart, the Central Plains fell into chaos, the Five Barbarians contended in turn, and the classics and their Way were exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: After the Jin dynasty fell apart, the Central Plains were lost to chaos, the Five Barbarian peoples fought one another in succession, and the canonical texts and the Way they embodied were all but destroyed.

sentences.zh: 魏氏發跡代陰，經營河朔，得之馬上，茲道未弘。

translations.literal: The Wei house rose from Dai in the north, took hold of the lands north of the Yellow River, won the realm from horseback, and this Way was not yet spread wide.
translations.idiomatic: The Wei rose from Dai in the north and secured the territory north of the Yellow River; having won the realm on horseback, they had not yet spread this teaching widely.

sentences.zh: 暨夫太和之後，盛修文教，搢紳碩學，濟濟盈朝，縫掖巨儒，往往傑出，其雅誥奧義，宋及齊、梁不能尚也。

translations.literal: From the Taihe reign onward they greatly cultivated literary teaching; gentry scholars and eminent learning filled the court in abundance, and great Confucians in scholar's robes often stood forth outstandingly. Their elegant pronouncements and profound meanings—Song, Qi, and Liang could not surpass them.
translations.idiomatic: From the Taihe era onward the court lavishly promoted literary and moral education; eminent scholars and great learning thronged the halls, and leading Confucians in scholar's robes rose to distinction again and again. In elegant exposition and profound doctrine, even Song, Qi, and Liang could not match them.

sentences.zh: 南北所治，章句好尚，互有不同。

translations.literal: What the south and north each upheld in commentarial learning and favored schools differed from one another.
translations.idiomatic: North and south each had its own commentarial traditions and favored schools of interpretation, and these differed markedly from one another.

sentences.zh: 江左《周易》則王輔嗣，《尚書》則孔安國，《左傳》則杜元凱。

translations.literal: In the lands east of the Yangzi, the Book of Changes followed Wang Fuzi, the Documents followed Kong Anguo, and the Zuo Commentary followed Du Yuankai.
translations.idiomatic: South of the Yangzi, the Book of Changes followed Wang Bi, the Documents Kong Anguo, and the Zuo Commentary Du Yu.

sentences.zh: 河、洛《左傳》則服子慎，《尚書》、《周易》則鄭康成。

translations.literal: In the Yellow River and Luo region the Zuo Commentary followed Fu Zishen, while the Documents and Book of Changes followed Zheng Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: In the Yellow River and Luo heartland the Zuo Commentary followed Fu Qian, while the Documents and Book of Changes followed Zheng Xuan.

sentences.zh: 《詩》則並主于毛公，《禮》則同遵于鄭氏。

translations.literal: The Odes on both sides took Master Mao as authority; the Rites on both sides alike followed the Zheng school.
translations.idiomatic: For the Odes both regions took Master Mao as authority; for the Rites both alike followed the Zheng school.

sentences.zh: 大抵南人約簡，得其英華，北學深蕪，窮其枝葉。

translations.literal: Broadly speaking, southerners were concise and grasped the essential brilliance; northern learning was deep but overgrown and exhausted the branches and leaves.
translations.idiomatic: Broadly speaking, southerners were concise and grasped the essential brilliance, while northern scholarship was deep but overgrown and pursued every branch and leaf of the text.

sentences.zh: 考其終始，要其會歸，其立身成名，殊方同致矣。

translations.literal: Examining their beginnings and ends and grasping their convergent aim, in establishing themselves and winning fame they reached the same end by different paths.
translations.idiomatic: When one weighs their beginnings and ends and grasps what they converged upon, in establishing themselves and winning renown they arrived at the same goal by different routes.

sentences.zh: 爰自漢、魏，碩學多清通，逮乎近古，巨儒必鄙俗。

translations.literal: From Han and Wei onward, eminent learning was mostly clear and penetrating; by recent antiquity, great Confucians were inevitably coarse and vulgar.
translations.idiomatic: From Han and Wei times onward, leading scholars were for the most part lucid and penetrating; in more recent ages, great Confucians have tended toward coarseness and vulgarity.

sentences.zh: 文、武不墜，弘之在人，豈獨愚蔽於當今，而皆明哲於往昔？

translations.literal: That culture and martial virtue do not fall depends on spreading them through people—are only those of today benighted, while all of the past were wise and clear-sighted?
translations.idiomatic: Whether civil and military culture endures depends on whether people carry it forward—can it be that only the present age is benighted while all past ages were wise?

sentences.zh: 在乎用與不用，知與不知耳。

translations.literal: It lies in employing or not employing them, in knowing or not knowing—that is all.
translations.idiomatic: The matter rests solely on whether they are employed or neglected, known or ignored.

sentences.zh: 然曩之弼諧庶績，必舉德于鴻儒，近代左右邦家，咸取士於刀筆。

translations.literal: Yet in former times those who aided and harmonized the myriad tasks always raised men of virtue from great Confucians; in recent times those who steer the state all take their officers from the brush and knife.
translations.idiomatic: Yet in former times those who aided the ruler in governing always promoted men of virtue from among great Confucians, whereas in recent times those who guide the state all recruit their officials from the ranks of clerks and scribes.

sentences.zh: 縱有學優入室，勤逾刺股，名高海內，擢第甲科，若命偶時來，未有望於青紫，或數將運舛，必委棄於草澤。

translations.literal: Even if one's learning entered the inner chamber, diligence surpassed pricking the thigh, fame towered within the seas, and one was selected in the top grade of the examinations—if fate happened to come at the right moment, one still had no hope of purple and scarlet rank; or if several generals met with ill fortune, one was sure to be cast off in the grasslands and marshes.
translations.idiomatic: Even when learning reached the highest mastery, diligence exceeded the student who pricked his thigh to stay awake, fame spread throughout the realm, and one placed first in the examinations—if fate and timing did not align, there was still no prospect of high office; and when several commanders fell from favor, one was inevitably abandoned to obscurity in the wilds.

sentences.zh: 然則古之學者，祿在其中，今之學者，困于貧賤。

translations.literal: Thus scholars of old had salary within their learning; scholars of today are trapped in poverty and low station.
translations.idiomatic: Thus scholars of old found stipend within their learning itself; scholars of today are trapped in poverty and low station.

sentences.zh: 明達之人，志識之士，安肯滯于所習，以求貧賤者哉？

translations.literal: How would the clear-sighted and men of purpose and insight willingly linger in what they have studied in order to seek poverty and low station?
translations.idiomatic: How could the clear-sighted and men of purpose willingly remain fixed in their studies only to court poverty and obscurity?

sentences.zh: 此所以儒罕通人，學多鄙俗者也。

translations.literal: This is why Confucians rarely produce penetrating men, and learning is mostly coarse and vulgar.
translations.idiomatic: This is why Confucians rarely produce truly accomplished scholars, and learning has grown coarse and vulgar.

sentences.zh: 昔齊列康莊之第，多士如林，燕起碣石之宮，群英自遠。

translations.literal: Formerly Qi set out mansions on the broad avenue and men of talent were thick as a forest; Yan raised the Jieshi palace and clusters of worthies came of themselves from afar.
translations.idiomatic: Formerly Qi lined mansions along the broad avenue and men of talent gathered thick as a forest; Yan raised the Jieshi palace and worthy men came of their own accord from far away.

sentences.zh: 是知俗易風移，必由上之所好，非夫聖明禦世，亦無以振斯頹俗矣。

translations.literal: From this one knows that customs change and winds shift only through what those above favor; unless a sage and enlightened ruler governs the age, there is likewise no means to revive this declining custom.
translations.idiomatic: From this one knows that customs change only according to what those above favor; unless a sage and enlightened ruler governs the age, there is no reviving a culture in such decline.

sentences.zh: 自正朔不一，將三百年，師說紛綸，無所取正。

translations.literal: From the time the calendar and regnal titles were not unified, for nearly three hundred years, masters' teachings were tangled and confused, with no standard to follow.
translations.idiomatic: For nearly three hundred years after the realm's calendars and regnal titles ceased to be unified, competing schools of interpretation proliferated with no authoritative standard to follow.

sentences.zh: 高祖膺期纂曆，平一寰宇，頓天網以掩之，賁旌帛以禮之，設好爵以縻之，於是四海九州強學待問之士，靡不畢集焉。

translations.literal: Emperor Gaozu received the mandate and succeeded to the calendar, pacified and unified the realm within the four seas, suddenly spread the heavenly net to cover them, honored them with patterned silks and ceremonial gifts, and set fine ranks to tether them—whereupon scholars eager to learn and awaiting inquiry from within the four seas and nine provinces all gathered without exception.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozu received Heaven's mandate and took up the imperial calendar, unified the realm, cast the wide net of rule over all, honored scholars with patterned silks and ritual gifts, and offered fine offices to hold them—whereupon eager students and questioners from every corner of the empire gathered without exception.

sentences.zh: 天子乃整萬乘，率百僚，遵問道之儀，觀釋奠之禮。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven then arrayed his ten thousand chariots, led the hundred officials, followed the rites of inquiring into the Way, and observed the ceremony of offering sacrifice at the end of mourning.
translations.idiomatic: The Son of Heaven then arrayed his imperial train, led the hundred officials, performed the rites of inquiring into the Way, and observed the libation sacrifice to Confucius.

sentences.zh: 博士罄懸河之辯，侍中竭重席之奧，考正亡逸，研核異同，積滯群疑，渙然冰釋。

translations.literal: Erudites exhausted the debate of a river suspended in air; attendants within the palace gates drained the profundities of layered mats; they examined and corrected what was lost or missing, investigated and verified differences and agreements, and piled-up doubts of the multitude dissolved like ice melting.
translations.idiomatic: Erudites poured forth eloquence like a river in flood; palace attendants plumbed the deepest teachings of the layered mat lectures; lost texts were collated and discrepancies weighed, until long-standing doubts melted away like ice in spring.

sentences.zh: 於是超擢奇秀，厚賞諸儒，京邑達乎四方，皆啟黌校。

translations.literal: Thereupon he promoted outstanding and exceptional men, richly rewarded the various Confucians, and from the capital reaching to the four quarters, all opened schoolhouses.
translations.idiomatic: Thereupon he promoted exceptional talent, richly rewarded the Confucians, and from the capital to the four quarters schoolhouses were opened everywhere.

sentences.zh: 齊、魯、趙、魏，學者尤多，負笈追師，不遠千里，講誦之聲，道路不絕。

translations.literal: In Qi, Lu, Zhao, and Wei scholars were especially numerous; bearing satchels they pursued teachers, not shunning a thousand li, and the sound of lecturing and recitation on the roads never ceased.
translations.idiomatic: In Qi, Lu, Zhao, and Wei scholars were especially numerous; carrying book-boxes they followed teachers for a thousand li without hesitation, and the sound of lecture and recitation never ceased along the roads.

sentences.zh: 中州儒雅之盛，自漢、魏以來，一時而已。

translations.literal: The flourishing of Confucian elegance in the Central Provinces, since Han and Wei, was only for a single age.
translations.idiomatic: The flowering of Confucian culture in the Central Provinces had not been seen in such fullness since Han and Wei times—yet it lasted only a moment.

sentences.zh: 及高祖暮年，精華稍竭，不悅儒術，專尚刑名，執政之徒，咸非篤好。

translations.literal: When Gaozu reached his later years his vital essence was somewhat exhausted; he did not delight in Confucian arts but devoted himself to penal statutes and names, and those in power were none of them devoted lovers of learning.
translations.idiomatic: When Gaozu reached his later years his vigor waned; he lost interest in Confucian learning and favored penal law instead, and none among those who held power were sincere patrons of scholarship.

sentences.zh: 既仁壽間，遂廢天下之學，唯存國子一所，弟子七十二人。

translations.literal: In the Renshou era he then abolished learning throughout the realm, keeping only the Directorate of Education with seventy-two disciples.
translations.idiomatic: During the Renshou era he abolished schools throughout the realm, retaining only the Imperial University with seventy-two students.

sentences.zh: 煬帝即位，復開庠序，國子郡縣之學，盛於開皇之初。

translations.literal: When Emperor Yang acceded, he reopened the schools; the Directorate of Education and the commandery and county schools flourished as at the beginning of Kaihuang.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Yang took the throne he reopened the schools, and the Imperial University together with commandery and county schools flourished as they had at the start of the Kaihuang era.

sentences.zh: 徵辟儒生，遠近畢至，使相與講論得失於東都之下，納言定其差次，一以聞奏焉。

translations.literal: He summoned and recruited Confucian scholars, who came from near and far; he had them debate gains and losses together below the Eastern Capital, and the Director of the Palace Secretariat fixed their ranking and reported all to the throne.
translations.idiomatic: He summoned Confucian scholars from near and far, had them debate the merits and flaws of competing interpretations below the Eastern Capital, and the Director of the Palace Secretariat ranked their conclusions and reported them all to the throne.

sentences.zh: 于時舊儒多已凋亡，二劉拔萃出類，學通南北，博極今古，後生鑽仰，莫之能測。

translations.literal: At that time the old Confucians had mostly withered away; the two Lius stood out from the crowd and surpassed their kind, their learning penetrating north and south and their breadth exhausting present and past—later students drilled into and looked up to them, and none could fathom them.
translations.idiomatic: By then most of the older Confucians had died off; the two Liu scholars stood head and shoulders above the rest, mastering learning from both north and south and ranging across all antiquity and their own age—later students studied under them in awe, and none could match their depth.

sentences.zh: 所制諸經義疏，搢紳咸師宗之。

translations.literal: The commentaries on meaning that they composed for the various classics were all taken as masters by the gentry.
translations.idiomatic: The exegetical commentaries they composed on the classics were adopted as authoritative by the entire scholarly elite.

sentences.zh: 既而外事四夷，戎馬不息，師徒怠散，盜賊群起，禮義不足以防君子，刑罰不足以威小人，空有建學之名，而無弘道之實。

translations.literal: Then he turned to external affairs with the four barbarians; war-horses never rested; teachers and students grew slack and scattered; bandits rose in groups; ritual and righteousness were insufficient to guard against gentlemen, and punishments were insufficient to awe petty men—there was only the name of establishing schools, without the reality of spreading the Way.
translations.idiomatic: Then foreign campaigns against the four quarters never ceased; teachers and students drifted apart; bandits rose everywhere; ritual and righteousness could no longer restrain the worthy, nor punishments awe the base—there remained only the name of founding schools, without the reality of spreading the Way.

sentences.zh: 其風漸墜，以至滅亡，方領矩步之徒，亦多轉死溝壑。

translations.literal: Its wind gradually fell, until extinction; those in square collars who measured their steps also mostly ended by dying in ditches and gullies.
translations.idiomatic: The tradition gradually collapsed until the dynasty itself perished, and many of those scholars in square collars who walked by measured steps likewise died in ditches and gullies.

sentences.zh: 凡有經籍，自此皆湮沒於煨塵矣。

translations.literal: All canonical texts from this time onward were buried and lost in smoldering dust.
translations.idiomatic: From that time forward the canonical texts were all buried and lost in ashes and dust.

sentences.zh: 遂使後進之士不復聞《詩》、《書》之言，皆懷攘奪之心，相與陷於不義。

translations.literal: Thus later students no longer heard the words of the Odes and Documents; all harbored hearts of seizure and plunder and together fell into unrighteousness.
translations.idiomatic: Thus the younger generation no longer heard the words of the Odes and Documents; all harbored hearts bent on seizure and plunder, and together they fell into unrighteousness.

sentences.zh: 《傳》曰：「學者將植，不學者將落。」

translations.literal: The Commentary says: "Those who study will be established; those who do not study will fall."
translations.idiomatic: The Commentary says: "Those who study will rise; those who do not study will fall."

sentences.zh: 然則盛衰是系，興亡攸在，有國有家者可不慎歟！

translations.literal: Thus prosperity and decline depend on this; rise and fall lie herein—can those who possess a state and a house fail to be cautious!
translations.idiomatic: Thus prosperity and decline hang upon it, and rise and fall depend upon it—how can rulers of states and clans fail to be cautious!

sentences.zh: 諸儒有身沒道存，遺風可想，皆采其餘論，綴之於此篇雲。

translations.literal: Among the various Confucians there were those whose bodies perished but whose Way remained; their lingering wind can still be imagined—all their remaining discourses are gathered and appended in this chapter.
translations.idiomatic: Among the Confucians were men whose bodies perished but whose teaching endured, whose lingering influence can still be imagined—their remaining writings are gathered and appended in this chapter.

sentences.zh: 元善元善，河南洛陽人也。

translations.literal: Yuan Shan. Yuan Shan was a native of Luoyang in Henan.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Shan was a native of Luoyang in Henan commandery.

sentences.zh: 祖叉，魏侍中。

translations.literal: His grandfather Cha was Attendant-in-Ordinary of Wei.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Cha served as Attendant-in-Ordinary under the Wei.

sentences.zh: 父羅，初為梁州刺史，及叉被誅，奔于梁，官至征北大將軍、青冀二州刺史。

translations.literal: His father Luo was at first Governor of Liang Province; when Cha was executed he fled to Liang and reached the posts of General Who Pacifies the North and Governor of Qing and Ji provinces.
translations.idiomatic: His father Luo was initially governor of Liang province; when Cha was executed he fled to the Liang court and rose to general who pacifies the north and governor of Qing and Ji provinces.

sentences.zh: 善少隨父至江南，性好學，遂通涉五經，尤明《左氏傳》。

translations.literal: Shan in his youth followed his father to the lands south of the Yangzi; by nature he loved learning and thus thoroughly mastered the Five Classics, especially excelling in the Zuo Commentary.
translations.idiomatic: In youth Shan followed his father south of the Yangzi; he loved learning by nature, mastered the Five Classics, and was especially expert in the Zuo Commentary.

sentences.zh: 及侯景之亂，善歸於周。

translations.literal: When the turmoil of Hou Jing came, Shan returned to Zhou.
translations.idiomatic: When the rebellion of Hou Jing broke out, Shan went over to Northern Zhou.

sentences.zh: 武帝甚禮之，以為太子宮尹，賜爵江陽縣公。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu treated him with great courtesy, made him Palace Tutor to the Heir Apparent, and enfeoffed him as Duke of Jiangyang county.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu treated him with great respect, appointed him tutor in the heir apparent's palace, and enfeoffed him as Duke of Jiangyang.

sentences.zh: 每執經以授太子。

translations.literal: Each time he held the classics to instruct the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: He regularly lectured on the classics for the crown prince.

sentences.zh: 開皇初，拜內史侍郎，上每望之曰：「人倫儀錶也。」

translations.literal: At the beginning of Kaihuang he was appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat; the emperor whenever he looked upon him said: "The model and measure of human relations."
translations.idiomatic: At the beginning of the Kaihuang era he was appointed vice director of the Imperial Secretariat; whenever the emperor saw him he would say, "The very model of human conduct."

sentences.zh: 凡有敷奏，詞氣抑揚，觀者屬目。

translations.literal: Whenever he presented memorials, the tone of his words rose and fell; those who watched fixed their eyes upon him.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever he presented memorials to the throne, his cadence rose and fell with such grace that all eyes in the hall were drawn to him.

sentences.zh: 陳使袁雅來聘，上令善就館受書，雅出門不拜。

translations.literal: The Chen envoy Yuan Ya came on a mission of courtesy; the emperor ordered Shan to go to the lodge to receive the letter of credence, and Ya went out the door without bowing.
translations.idiomatic: When the Chen envoy Yuan Ya came on a diplomatic mission, the emperor ordered Shan to receive his credentials at the guest lodge; Ya left the door without performing a bow.

sentences.zh: 善論舊事有拜之儀，雅不能對，遂拜，成禮而去。

translations.literal: Shan argued that by old precedent there was a rite of bowing; Ya could not reply, and so bowed, completed the ceremony, and departed.
translations.idiomatic: Shan argued that precedent required a bow on such occasions; Ya could not answer, performed the bow, completed the ceremony, and departed.

sentences.zh: 後遷國子祭酒。

translations.literal: Later he was transferred to be Chancellor of the Directorate of Education.
translations.idiomatic: He was later appointed chancellor of the Imperial University.

sentences.zh: 上嘗親臨釋奠，命善講《孝經》。

translations.literal: The emperor once personally attended the libation sacrifice and ordered Shan to lecture on the Classic of Filial Piety.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor once attended the libation sacrifice in person and ordered Shan to lecture on the Classic of Filial Piety.

sentences.zh: 於是敷陳義理，兼之以諷諫。

translations.literal: Thereupon he spread forth the principles of meaning and added admonition by indirect criticism.
translations.idiomatic: He thereupon expounded the text's principles and wove in indirect admonition of the throne.

sentences.zh: 上大悅曰：「聞江陽之說，更起朕心。」

translations.literal: The emperor was greatly pleased and said: "Hearing the discourse of Jiangyang has renewed my heart."
translations.idiomatic: The emperor was greatly pleased and said, "Hearing the Duke of Jiangyang's lecture has stirred my heart anew."

sentences.zh: 賚絹百匹，衣一襲。

translations.literal: He bestowed a hundred bolts of silk and one suit of clothing.
translations.idiomatic: He rewarded him with a hundred bolts of silk and a suit of robes.

sentences.zh: 善之通博，在何妥之下，然以風流醖藉，俯仰可觀，音韻清朗，聽者忘倦，由是為後進所歸。

translations.literal: Shan's breadth of mastery was below He Tuo's, yet by his elegant bearing and refined ease, his deportment in rising and bowing was a sight to behold, his tones clear and resonant so that listeners forgot weariness—thereby he became the object to which later students turned.
translations.idiomatic: Shan's erudition ranked below He Tuo's, yet his bearing was elegant and refined, his gestures pleasing to watch, and his voice so clear that listeners forgot fatigue—thus later students flocked to him.

sentences.zh: 妥每懷不平，心欲屈善。

translations.literal: Tuo always harbored resentment and in his heart wished to humble Shan.
translations.idiomatic: Tuo always nursed resentment and wished to humble Shan.

sentences.zh: 因善講《春秋》，初發題，諸儒畢集。

translations.literal: When Shan was to lecture on the Spring and Autumn Annals and first opened the topic, all the Confucians gathered.
translations.idiomatic: When Shan was to lecture on the Spring and Autumn Annals and first announced his theme, all the Confucian scholars gathered.

sentences.zh: 善私謂妥曰：「名望已定，幸無相苦。」

translations.literal: Shan privately said to Tuo: "Fame and standing are already fixed—please do not make things hard for me."
translations.idiomatic: Shan privately said to Tuo, "My reputation is already established—please do not make things difficult for me."

sentences.zh: 妥然之。

translations.literal: Tuo assented.
translations.idiomatic: Tuo agreed.

sentences.zh: 及就講肆，妥遂引古今滯義以難，善多不能對。

translations.literal: When they came to the lecture hall, Tuo then cited obscure points of meaning from past and present to challenge him, and Shan often could not reply.
translations.idiomatic: When they entered the lecture hall, Tuo cited knotty points of interpretation from antiquity and the present to challenge him, and Shan often could not answer.

sentences.zh: 善深銜之，二人由是有隙。

translations.literal: Shan deeply harbored resentment, and from this the two men had a rift.
translations.idiomatic: Shan deeply resented this, and from that time the two men were at odds.

sentences.zh: 善以高熲有宰相之具，嘗言於上曰：「楊素粗疏，蘇威怯芃，元胄、元旻，正似鴨耳。

translations.literal: Shan considered Gao Jiong to possess the makings of a chief minister and once said to the emperor: "Yang Su is coarse and careless, Su Wei is timid and weak, Yuan Zhou and Yuan Min are just like ducks.
translations.idiomatic: Shan believed Gao Jiong had the makings of a chief minister and once told the emperor, "Yang Su is crude and careless, Su Wei timid and irresolute, and Yuan Zhou and Yuan Min are no better than ducks.

sentences.zh: 可以付社稷者，唯獨高熲。」

translations.literal: The one to whom the altars of state can be entrusted is Gao Jiong alone."
translations.idiomatic: Only Gao Jiong can be entrusted with the altars of state."

sentences.zh: 上初然之，及熲得罪，上以善之言為熲遊說，深責望之。

translations.literal: The emperor at first agreed; when Jiong fell from grace, the emperor took Shan's words as pleading on Jiong's behalf and deeply blamed and reproached him.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor at first agreed; when Jiong fell from favor the emperor took Shan's words as lobbying on Jiong's behalf and blamed him severely.

sentences.zh: 善憂懼，先患消渴，於是疾動而卒，時年六十。

translations.literal: Shan was anxious and fearful; he had long suffered from wasting thirst, and now his illness flared and he died, aged sixty.
translations.idiomatic: Shan grew anxious and afraid; he had long suffered from diabetes, his illness suddenly worsened, and he died at the age of sixty.

sentences.zh: 辛彥之辛彥之，隴西狄道人也。

translations.literal: Xin Yanzhi. Xin Yanzhi was a native of Didao in Longxi.
translations.idiomatic: Xin Yanzhi was a native of Didao in Longxi commandery.

sentences.zh: 祖世敘，魏涼州刺史。

translations.literal: His grandfather Shixu was Governor of Liang Province under Wei.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Shixu was governor of Liang province under the Wei.

sentences.zh: 父靈輔，周滑州刺史。

translations.literal: His father Lingfu was Governor of Hua Province under Zhou.
translations.idiomatic: His father Lingfu was governor of Hua province under Northern Zhou.

sentences.zh: 彥之九歲而孤，不交非類，博涉經史，與天水牛弘同志好學。

translations.literal: Yanzhi was orphaned at nine; he did not associate with unworthy sorts, broadly mastered the classics and histories, and with Niu Hong of Tianshui shared the same ambition and love of learning.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi was orphaned at nine; he kept company only with worthy men, mastered the classics and histories, and shared a passion for learning with Niu Hong of Tianshui.

sentences.zh: 後入關，遂家京兆。

translations.literal: Later he entered the passes and made his home in Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Later he entered the Guanzhong region and settled his household in the capital district.

sentences.zh: 周太祖見而器之，引為中外府禮曹，賜以衣馬珠玉。

translations.literal: Emperor Taizu of Zhou saw him and valued his talent, drew him in as an officer of Rites in the Central and Outer Bureau, and bestowed clothing, horses, pearls, and jade.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Taizu of Zhou recognized his talent, appointed him to the rites office of the central administration, and rewarded him with robes, horses, pearls, and jade.

sentences.zh: 時國家草創，百度伊始，朝貴多出武人，修定儀注，唯彥之而已。

translations.literal: At that time the state was newly founded and the hundred offices just beginning; court nobles mostly came from military men—only Yanzhi revised and fixed ritual regulations.
translations.idiomatic: The state was newly founded and every institution was being established from scratch; most court nobles were military men, and Yanzhi alone was charged with revising ritual regulations.

sentences.zh: 尋拜中書侍郎。

translations.literal: Soon he was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon appointed vice director of the Secretariat.

sentences.zh: 及周閔帝受禪，彥之與少宗伯盧辯專掌儀制。

translations.literal: When Emperor Min of Zhou received the abdication, Yanzhi together with the Vice Director of the Imperial Clan Lu Bian exclusively managed ritual institutions.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Min of Zhou accepted the abdication, Yanzhi and the vice director of the imperial clan Lu Bian were put solely in charge of ritual institutions.

sentences.zh: 明、武時，曆職典祀，太祝、樂部、禦正四曹大夫，開府儀同三司。

translations.literal: Under Emperors Ming and Wu he successively held offices in charge of sacrifices: Grand Invocator, Director of the Music Office, Director of the Four Offices of Imperial Rectitude, and Grand Master with Golden Seal and Purse Opening the Office with Equipage Equal to a Three-Ducal Minister.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperors Ming and Wu he held successive posts overseeing sacrifices—grand invocator, director of music, director of the four offices of imperial rectitude—and rose to grand master with golden seal and privileges equal to a three-ducal minister.

sentences.zh: 奉使迎突厥皇后還，賚馬二百匹，賜爵龍門縣公，邑千戶。

translations.literal: On a mission to welcome back the Tujue empress he was rewarded with two hundred horses, enfeoffed as Duke of Longmen county with a fief of a thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: On a mission to escort the Türk empress back he was rewarded with two hundred horses and enfeoffed as Duke of Longmen with a fief of one thousand households.

sentences.zh: 尋進爵五原郡公，加邑千戶。

translations.literal: Soon his rank was advanced to Duke of Wuyuan commandery with an additional thousand households in the fief.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon promoted to duke of Wuyuan commandery with an additional thousand households added to his fief.

sentences.zh: 宣帝即位，拜少宗伯。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuan acceded he was appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Clan.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan took the throne he was appointed vice director of the imperial clan.

sentences.zh: 高祖受禪，除太常少卿，改封任城郡公，進位上開府。

translations.literal: When Gaozu received the abdication he was dismissed to be Vice Minister of Imperial Sacrifices, re-enfeoffed as Duke of Rencheng commandery, and advanced to Upper Purse-Opening Office.
translations.idiomatic: When Gaozu accepted the abdication he was appointed vice minister of imperial sacrifices, re-enfeoffed as duke of Rencheng commandery, and promoted to upper purse-opening office.

sentences.zh: 尋轉國子祭酒。

translations.literal: Soon he was transferred to be Chancellor of the Directorate of Education.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon transferred to chancellor of the Imperial University.

sentences.zh: 歲餘，拜禮部尚書，與秘書監牛弘撰《新禮》。

translations.literal: After more than a year he was appointed Minister of Rites and together with Niu Hong, Director of the Imperial Library, compiled the New Rites.
translations.idiomatic: After more than a year he was appointed minister of rites and, together with Niu Hong, director of the imperial library, compiled the New Rites.

sentences.zh: 吳興沈重名為碩學，高祖嘗令彥之與重論議，重不能抗，於是避席而謝曰：「辛君所謂金城湯池，無可攻之勢。」

translations.literal: Shen Chong of Wuxing was famed as a great scholar; Gaozu once had Yanzhi debate with Chong, and Chong could not withstand him—thereupon he left his mat and apologized, saying: "Master Xin is what they call a golden rampart and boiling moat, with no position that can be attacked."
translations.idiomatic: Shen Chong of Wuxing was famed as a leading scholar; Gaozu once had Yanzhi debate him, and Chong could not hold his ground—he rose from his seat and said, "Master Xin is a golden rampart and boiling moat; there is no point of attack."

sentences.zh: 高祖大悅。

translations.literal: Gaozu was greatly pleased.
translations.idiomatic: Gaozu was greatly pleased.

sentences.zh: 後拜隨州刺史。

translations.literal: Later he was appointed Governor of Sui Province.
translations.idiomatic: He was later appointed governor of Sui province.

sentences.zh: 于時州牧多貢珍玩，唯彥之所貢，並供祭之物。

translations.literal: At that time provincial governors mostly presented rare curios; only what Yanzhi presented consisted entirely of objects for sacrifice.
translations.idiomatic: At that time most provincial governors sent rare curios as tribute; Yanzhi alone sent only items for ritual sacrifice.

sentences.zh: 高祖善之，顧謂朝臣曰：「人安得無學！

translations.literal: Gaozu approved of this and, turning to the court officials, said: "How can a man do without learning!
translations.idiomatic: Gaozu approved and, turning to the court, said, "How can a man do without learning!

sentences.zh: 彥之所貢，稽古之力也。」

translations.literal: What Yanzhi presented is the power of investigating antiquity."
translations.idiomatic: What Yanzhi presents is the fruit of studying antiquity."

sentences.zh: 遷潞州刺史，前後俱有惠政。

translations.literal: He was transferred to be Governor of Lu Province; in both posts he had benevolent administration.
translations.idiomatic: He was transferred to governor of Lu province, and in both posts governed with benevolence.

sentences.zh: 彥之又崇信佛道，於城內立浮圖二所，並十五層。

translations.literal: Yanzhi also revered the Buddhist Way and within the city erected two pagodas, each of fifteen stories.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi also devoutly practiced Buddhism and built two fifteen-story pagodas within the city.

sentences.zh: 開皇十一年，州人張元暴死，數日乃蘇，雲遊天上，見新構一堂，制極崇麗。

translations.literal: In the eleventh year of Kaihuang the man of the province Zhang Yuan died suddenly; after several days he revived and said he had wandered in Heaven and seen a newly built hall of extremely lofty and beautiful design.
translations.idiomatic: In the eleventh year of Kaihuang a local man named Zhang Yuan died suddenly; after several days he revived and said he had wandered in Heaven and seen a newly built hall of surpassing splendor.

sentences.zh: 元問其故，人云潞州刺史辛彥之有功德，造此堂以待之。

translations.literal: Yuan asked the reason, and someone said that Xin Yanzhi, Governor of Lu Province, had merit and virtue and had built this hall to await him.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan asked the reason and was told that Xin Yanzhi, governor of Lu province, had accumulated merit and that the hall had been built to await him.

sentences.zh: 彥之聞而不悅。

translations.literal: When Yanzhi heard of it he was not pleased.
translations.idiomatic: When Yanzhi heard this he was displeased.

sentences.zh: 其年卒官。

translations.literal: That same year he died in office.
translations.idiomatic: That same year he died in office.

sentences.zh: 諡曰宣。

translations.literal: His posthumous title was Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: He was posthumously named Xuan.

sentences.zh: 彥之撰《墳典》一部，《六官》一部，《祝文》一部，《新要》一部，《新禮》一部，《五經異義》一部，並行於世。

translations.literal: Yanzhi compiled one work each of the *Fendian*, *Liuguan*, *Zhuwen*, *Xinyao*, *Xinli*, and *Wujing Yiyi*, all of which circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi authored six works—the *Fendian*, *Liuguan*, *Zhuwen*, *Xinyao*, *Xinli*, and *Wujing Yiyi*—all of which circulated widely.

sentences.zh: 有子仲龕，官至猗氏令。

translations.literal: He had a son Zhongkan, who reached the office of magistrate of Yishi.
translations.idiomatic: He had a son named Zhongkan, who rose to become magistrate of Yishi county.

sentences.zh: 何妥 蕭該 包愷何妥，字棲鳳，西城人也。

translations.literal: He Tuo. Xiao Gai. Bao Kai. He Tuo, courtesy name Qifeng, was a native of Xicheng.
translations.idiomatic: [He Tuo. Xiao Gai. Bao Kai.] He Tuo, courtesy name Qifeng, was a native of Xicheng.

sentences.zh: 父細胡，通商入蜀，遂家郫縣，事梁武陵王妃，主知金帛，因致巨富，號為西州大賈。

translations.literal: His father Xihu traded and entered Shu, then made his home in Pixian; he served the consort of Prince Wuling of Liang, was in charge of gold and silk, and thereby amassed great wealth, being called the great merchant of the Western Prefecture.
translations.idiomatic: His father Xihu was a merchant who traveled into Shu and settled in Pixian county. He served the consort of Liang's Prince of Wuling, managed gold and silk accounts, amassed a vast fortune, and was known as the great merchant of the west.

sentences.zh: 妥少機警，八歲游國子學，助教顧良戲之曰：「汝既姓何，是荷葉之荷，為是河水之河？」

translations.literal: Tuo in youth was quick-witted; at eight he studied at the Imperial Academy, and Assistant Teacher Gu Liang teased him, saying: "Since your surname is He, is it the he of lotus leaf, or the he of river water?
translations.idiomatic: Tuo was sharp and clever from childhood. At eight he entered the Imperial Academy, where Assistant Instructor Gu Liang teased him: "Your surname is He—is that the he of lotus leaf, or the he of river water?

sentences.zh: 應聲答曰：「先生姓顧，是眷顧之顧，是新故之故？」

translations.literal: He answered at once: "Sir, your surname is Gu—is it the gu of to regard fondly, or the gu of old and new?"
translations.idiomatic: Tuo replied without hesitation: "Sir, your surname is Gu—is that the gu of 'to look upon fondly,' or the gu of 'old and new'?"

sentences.zh: 眾咸異之。

translations.literal: The whole assembly marveled at this.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone present was astonished.

sentences.zh: 十七，以技巧事湘東王，後知其聰明，召為誦書左右。

translations.literal: At seventeen, through skill and talent he served the Prince of Xiangdong; afterward the prince came to know his intelligence and summoned him as a recitation attendant at his side.
translations.idiomatic: At seventeen he entered the service of the Prince of Xiangdong through his talents; when the prince recognized his intelligence, he was made a recitation attendant at the prince's side.

sentences.zh: 時蘭陵蕭該亦有俊才，住青楊巷，妥住白楊頭，時人為之語曰：「世有兩俊，白楊何妥，青楊蕭該。」

translations.literal: At that time Xiao Gai of Lanling also had outstanding talent; he lived on Qingyang Lane and Tuo lived at Baiyangtou, and people of the time made a saying: "The age has two outstanding men—Baiyang He Tuo, Qingyang Xiao Gai.
translations.idiomatic: Xiao Gai of Lanling was also a man of outstanding talent; he lived on Qingyang Lane while Tuo lived at Baiyangtou, and people said: "The age boasts two brilliant minds—He Tuo of Baiyangtou, Xiao Gai of Qingyang Lane.

sentences.zh: 其見美如此。

translations.literal: Thus highly was he esteemed.
translations.idiomatic: Such was the esteem in which he was held.

sentences.zh: 江陵陷，周武帝尤重之，授太學博士。

translations.literal: When Jiangling fell, Emperor Wu of Zhou especially valued him and appointed him Erudite of the Grand Academy.
translations.idiomatic: After the fall of Jiangling, Emperor Wu of Zhou held him in special regard and appointed him Erudite of the Grand Academy.

sentences.zh: 宣帝初欲立五後，以問儒者辛彥之，對曰：「後與天子匹體齊尊，不宜有五。」

translations.literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xuan's reign, when he wished to establish five empresses, he asked the Confucian Xin Yanzhi, who replied: "An empress shares the body and equal dignity with the Son of Heaven—there should not be five.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Emperor Xuan's reign, when he proposed establishing five empresses, he consulted the Confucian scholar Xin Yanzhi, who answered: "An empress shares the Son of Heaven's dignity as his equal in rank—it is not fitting to have five.

sentences.zh: 妥駁曰：「帝嚳四妃，舜又二妃，亦何常數？」

translations.literal: Tuo rebutted: "Emperor Ku had four consorts, and Shun again had two consorts—where is the fixed number?"
translations.idiomatic: Tuo objected: "Emperor Ku had four consorts, and Shun had two—what fixed number is there?"

sentences.zh: 由是封襄城縣伯。

translations.literal: Thereupon he was enfeoffed as Baron of Xiangcheng county.
translations.idiomatic: For this he was enfeoffed as Baron of Xiangcheng county.

sentences.zh: 高祖受禪，除國子博士，加通直散騎常侍，進爵為公。

translations.literal: When Gaozu received the abdication, Tuo was appointed Erudite of the National University, additionally given the post of Tongzhi Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Sanqi Section, and his rank was advanced to duke.
translations.idiomatic: When Gaozu accepted the throne, Tuo was appointed Erudite of the National University, made Tongzhi Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Sanqi Section, and promoted to duke.

sentences.zh: 妥性勁急，有口才，好是非人物。

translations.literal: Tuo by nature was stern and quick-tempered, had eloquence, and liked to pass judgment on others.
translations.idiomatic: Tuo was stern and quick-tempered by nature, eloquent of tongue, and fond of finding fault with others.

sentences.zh: 時納言蘇威嘗言於上曰：「臣先人每誡臣雲，唯讀《孝經》一卷，足可立身治國，何用多為！」

translations.literal: At that time the Palace Aide Su Wei once said to the emperor: "My forebear often admonished me, saying that reading only one volume of the *Classic of Filial Piety* is sufficient to establish oneself and govern the state—what need is there to do more!
translations.idiomatic: At the time Palace Aide Su Wei once told the emperor: "My forebear often warned me that a single volume of the *Classic of Filial Piety* is enough to conduct oneself and govern the realm—what need for more?

sentences.zh: 上亦然之。

translations.literal: The emperor also agreed with this.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor agreed.

sentences.zh: 妥進曰：「蘇威所學，非止《孝經》。

translations.literal: Tuo stepped forward and said: "What Su Wei has studied is not limited to the *Classic of Filial Piety* alone.
translations.idiomatic: Tuo spoke up: "Su Wei's learning extends far beyond the *Classic of Filial Piety*.

sentences.zh: 厥父若信有此言，威不從訓，是其不孝。

translations.literal: If his father truly said this and Wei did not follow the instruction, that is unfilial conduct on his part.
translations.idiomatic: If his father truly spoke thus and Wei failed to follow that teaching, he is unfilial.

sentences.zh: 若無此言，面欺陛下，是其不誠。

translations.literal: If there was no such saying, then to tell it to the emperor's face is deception on his part.
translations.idiomatic: If no such words were ever spoken, then telling Your Majesty so to his face is deceit.

sentences.zh: 不誠不孝，何以事君！

translations.literal: Deceitful and unfilial—how can such a one serve his lord!
translations.idiomatic: Neither sincere nor filial—how can such a man serve his sovereign!

sentences.zh: 且夫子有云：'不讀《詩》無以言，不讀《禮》無以立。

translations.literal: Moreover the Master said: "Without reading the *Odes* one cannot speak; without reading the *Rites* one cannot stand."
translations.idiomatic: Moreover the Master said: "Without studying the *Odes*, one has nothing to say; without studying the *Rites*, one has no firm footing."

sentences.zh: '豈容蘇綽教子獨反聖人之訓乎？」

translations.literal: How can Su Chuo alone, in teaching his son, go against the sage's instruction?
translations.idiomatic: Can Su Chuo alone, in instructing his son, presume to contradict the sage's teaching?

sentences.zh: 威時兼領五職，上甚親重之，妥因奏威不可信任。

translations.literal: Wei at the time concurrently held five offices, and the emperor was very close to and valued him; Tuo accordingly memorialized that Wei could not be trusted.
translations.idiomatic: Su Wei at the time held five concurrent posts, and the emperor held him in close regard; Tuo thereupon submitted a memorial declaring Wei unworthy of trust.

sentences.zh: 又以掌天文律度，皆不稱職，妥又上八事以諫：

translations.literal: Further, because Wei managed astronomy and musical pitch but was not competent in either, Tuo again submitted eight items as remonstrance:
translations.idiomatic: He also charged that Wei, though charged with astronomy and the regulation of pitch, was incompetent in both, and submitted an eight-point memorial of remonstrance:

sentences.zh: 其一事曰：臣聞知人則哲，惟帝難之。

translations.literal: The first item says: I have heard that to know men is to be wise, yet it is the emperor alone for whom this is difficult.
translations.idiomatic: The first point reads: I have heard that to know men is wisdom, yet this is what the emperor alone finds difficult.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「舉直錯諸枉則民服，舉枉錯諸直則民不服。」

translations.literal: Confucius said: "Raise the upright and place them above the crooked, and the people will submit; raise the crooked and place them above the upright, and the people will not submit.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said: "Promote the upright and set them above the crooked, and the people will be compliant; promote the crooked and set them above the upright, and the people will not comply.

sentences.zh: 由此言之，政之治亂，必慎所舉，故進賢受上賞，蔽賢蒙顯戮。

translations.literal: From this it follows that in governing, order or disorder depends on whom one appoints; hence advancing the worthy receives the highest reward, while concealing the worthy suffers conspicuous punishment.
translations.idiomatic: From this it follows that whether government is well or ill ordered depends entirely on whom one appoints; thus those who advance the worthy earn the highest reward, while those who conceal talent face conspicuous punishment.

sentences.zh: 察今之舉人，良異於此，無論諂直，莫擇賢愚。

translations.literal: Observing those promoted today, it differs greatly from this: regardless of flattery or integrity, none distinguishes the worthy from the fool.
translations.idiomatic: Today, however, the practice of promotion differs sharply: no distinction is made between flatterers and upright men, worthy talent and mediocrity.

sentences.zh: 心欲崇高，則起家喉舌之任；

translations.literal: If one wishes in heart to rise high, then one begins with the role of spokesman;
translations.idiomatic: If one aspires to rise quickly, one starts out in a spokesman's post;

sentences.zh: 意須抑屈，必白首郎署之官。

translations.literal: If one's intent must be suppressed and bent down, then one ends as a white-haired clerk in a minor bureau.
translations.idiomatic: if one must be held down, one ends a white-haired clerk in some minor bureau.

sentences.zh: 人之不服，實由於此。

translations.literal: The people's failure to submit truly stems from this.
translations.idiomatic: The people's resentment stems precisely from this.

sentences.zh: 臣聞爵人於朝，與士共之，刑人於市，與眾棄之。

translations.literal: I have heard that ennobling a man is done at court, shared with officials; punishing a man is done in the market, abandoned by the multitude.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard that conferring rank is done at court, shared with the nobility, while inflicting punishment is done in the marketplace, abandoned to public contempt.

sentences.zh: 伏見留心獄訟，愛人如子，每應決獄，無不詢訪群公，刑之不濫，君之明也。

translations.literal: I humbly observe that Your Majesty attends carefully to lawsuits, loving the people as one's children; whenever a case is decided, you invariably consult the high ministers—punishment is not applied wantonly: this is the ruler's wisdom.
translations.idiomatic: I observe that Your Majesty attends carefully to the courts, loving the people as a father loves his children; before rendering judgment you always consult your ministers, and punishment is never meted out arbitrarily—this is the mark of a wise sovereign.

sentences.zh: 刑既如此，爵亦宜然。

translations.literal: Since punishment is so handled, ennoblement should likewise be so.
translations.idiomatic: If punishment is handled thus, the conferring of rank should follow the same principle.

sentences.zh: 若有懋功簡在帝心者，便可擢用。

translations.literal: If there is one whose outstanding merit has been noted in the emperor's heart, he may be promoted and employed at once.
translations.idiomatic: When someone of outstanding merit has already won Your Majesty's notice, he may be promoted directly.

sentences.zh: 自斯以降，若選重官，必須參以眾議，勿信一人之舉；

translations.literal: From that level downward, if selecting for important office, one must consult the opinion of the multitude—do not trust a single person's recommendation;
translations.idiomatic: For all lesser appointments, important posts must be filled only after consultation with many voices—never on the recommendation of a single individual;

sentences.zh: 則上不偏私，下無怨望。

translations.literal: Then above there will be no partiality, and below there will be no resentment.
translations.idiomatic: Then there will be no favoritism above and no resentment below.

sentences.zh: 其二事曰：孔子云：「是察阿黨，則罪無掩蔽。」

translations.literal: The second item says: Confucius said: "If one examines factional cliques, then crimes cannot be concealed.
translations.idiomatic: The second point reads: Confucius said: "If one scrutinizes factions and cliques, then wrongdoing cannot be hidden.

sentences.zh: 又曰：「君子周而不比，小人比而不周。」

translations.literal: He also said: "The gentleman is inclusive but does not form factions; the petty man forms factions but is not inclusive."
translations.idiomatic: He also said: "The gentleman is inclusive without forming cliques; the petty man forms cliques without being truly inclusive."

sentences.zh: 所謂比者，即阿黨也。

translations.literal: What is called forming factions is precisely factional cliquishness.
translations.idiomatic: What is meant by forming factions is precisely this cliquish behavior.

sentences.zh: 謂心之所愛，既已光華榮顯，猶加提挈；

translations.literal: It means that those whom the heart favors, though already shining in glory and distinction, are still further lifted up;
translations.idiomatic: Those whom one favors, though already glittering in rank and honor, are promoted still further;

sentences.zh: 心之所惡，既已沈滯屈辱，薄言必怒。

translations.literal: Those whom the heart hates, though already sunk in stagnation and humiliation, at the slightest word are met with wrath.
translations.idiomatic: while those one despises, though already sunk in obscurity and humiliation, are provoked to anger at the slightest remark.

sentences.zh: 提挈既成，必相掩蔽，則欺上之心生矣；

translations.literal: Once such lifting up is accomplished, they necessarily conceal one another, and then the heart to deceive one's superiors arises;
translations.idiomatic: Once such favoritism takes hold, mutual concealment follows, and the will to deceive one's superiors emerges;

sentences.zh: 屈辱既加，則有怨恨，謗讟之言出矣。

translations.literal: Once humiliation is heaped on, there is resentment, and slanderous speech issues forth.
translations.idiomatic: once humiliation is piled on, resentment grows and slander spreads.

sentences.zh: 伏願廣加逖訪，勿使朋黨路開，威恩自任。

translations.literal: I humbly wish that Your Majesty would broadly extend inquiry far and wide, and not allow the path of faction to open, with authority and favor entrusted to oneself alone.
translations.idiomatic: I pray that Your Majesty will cast a wide net in inquiry and not let the path of faction remain open, with power and favor exercised at one's own discretion.

sentences.zh: 有國之患，莫大於此。

translations.literal: For one who possesses a state, there is no calamity greater than this.
translations.idiomatic: For a state, there is no affliction greater than this.

sentences.zh: 其三事曰：臣聞舜舉十六族，所謂八元、八愷也。

translations.literal: The third item says: I have heard that Shun raised up sixteen clans, the so-called Eight Worthies and Eight Virtuous Ones.
translations.idiomatic: The third point reads: I have heard that Shun elevated sixteen clans—the so-called Eight Worthies and Eight Good Men.

sentences.zh: 計其賢明，理優今日，猶復擇才授任，不相侵濫，故得四門雍穆，庶績咸熙。

translations.literal: Considering their worth and wisdom, though logically superior to those of today, he still selected talent and assigned offices without mutual encroachment or excess, and thereby achieved the four gates in harmonious dignity and all achievements flourishing.
translations.idiomatic: Even though their worth exceeded anything we know today, Shun still selected the best talent for each post without overlapping appointments—and so the four quarters lived in harmony and every task flourished.

sentences.zh: 今官員極多，用人甚少，有一人身上乃兼數職，為是國無人也？

translations.literal: Today officials are extremely numerous yet men employed are very few; one person on his person holds several offices—is it because the state has no men?
translations.idiomatic: Today there are vast numbers of official posts but very few men appointed to them; one person often holds several concurrent posts—is it because the state lacks talent?

sentences.zh: 為是人不善也？

translations.literal: Or is it because the men are not competent?
translations.idiomatic: Or because the men appointed are simply not up to the work?

sentences.zh: 今萬乘大國，髦彥不少，縱有明哲，無由自達。

translations.literal: Today in this great state of ten thousand chariots, outstanding talents are not few; even if there are wise and perspicacious men, they have no means to reach forward on their own.
translations.idiomatic: In a great realm of ten thousand chariots, outstanding men are hardly scarce; yet even the wise and perceptive have no path to advance on their own.

sentences.zh: 東方朔言曰：「尊之則為將，卑之則為虜。」

translations.literal: Dongfang Shuo said: "Honor him and he becomes a general; degrade him and he becomes a captive.
translations.idiomatic: Dongfang Shuo said: "Treat a man with honor and he becomes a general; treat him with contempt and he becomes a captive.

sentences.zh: 斯言信矣。

translations.literal: This saying is indeed true.
translations.idiomatic: How true those words are.

sentences.zh: 今當官之人，不度德量力，既無呂望、傅說之能，自負傅岩、滋水之氣，不慮憂深責重，唯畏總領不多，安斯寵任，輕彼權軸，好致顛蹶，實此之由。

translations.literal: Today's office-holders do not measure virtue and weigh capacity; lacking the ability of Lü Wang and Fu Yue, they nevertheless assume the aura of Fu Yan and Zishui, do not consider that deep is the worry and heavy the responsibility, but only fear that their overall command is not great enough—they rest content in such favored appointment, lightly regard that axis of power, and readily bring on collapse: truly it is from this.
translations.idiomatic: Today's officeholders do not measure their own virtue and capacity; lacking the ability of Lü Wang or Fu Yue, they nevertheless assume the destiny of men discovered at Fu Yan or Zishui. They give no thought to the weight of responsibility that comes with high office, worrying only that their portfolio is not large enough. Content with such favor, they treat the levers of power lightly—and disaster follows. This is the root cause.

sentences.zh: 《易》曰：「鼎折足，覆公餗，其形渥，凶。」

translations.literal: The *Changes* says: "The cauldron's legs break, overturning the lord's stew; its form is damp—misfortune.
translations.idiomatic: The *Book of Changes* says: "The cauldron's legs snap, spilling the lord's feast; its form is disgraced—this is misfortune.

sentences.zh: 言不勝其任也。

translations.literal: This speaks of not being equal to one's task.
translations.idiomatic: This means being unequal to one's duties.

sentences.zh: 臣聞窮力舉重，不能為用。

translations.literal: I have heard that exhausting one's strength to lift a heavy weight means one cannot be used.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard that one who strains every muscle to lift a weight too heavy for him is fit for no task at all.

sentences.zh: 伏願更任賢良，分才參掌，使各行有餘力，則庶事康哉。

translations.literal: I humbly wish that Your Majesty would reassign worthy and good men, divide talents to share in management, so that each in his line has surplus strength—then the myriad affairs would be well ordered.
translations.idiomatic: I pray that Your Majesty will appoint worthy men afresh, divide responsibilities according to talent, and give each man room to spare in his duties—then all affairs would prosper.

sentences.zh: 其四事曰：臣聞《禮》云：「析言破律，亂名改作，執左道以亂政者殺。」

translations.literal: The fourth item says: I have heard the *Rites* say: "Those who parse words to break laws, disorder names to innovate, and hold to heterodox ways to disturb government—kill them.
translations.idiomatic: The fourth point reads: I have heard the *Rites* declare: "Those who split hairs to break the law, disturb established names with reckless innovation, and practice heterodox ways to throw government into chaos—such men are to be put to death.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「仍舊貫，何必改作。」

translations.literal: Confucius said: "Follow the old pattern—why must one change and innovate?"
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said: "Keep to the old ways—why must everything be reinvented?"

sentences.zh: 伏見比年以來，改作者多矣。

translations.literal: I humbly observe that in recent years innovators have been many.
translations.idiomatic: I observe that in recent years the innovators have grown numerous.

sentences.zh: 至如範威漏刻，十載不成；

translations.literal: For example, Fan Wei's water clock—ten years and it was not completed;
translations.idiomatic: Fan Wei's clepsydra took ten years and still was not finished;

sentences.zh: 趙翊尺稱，七年方決。

translations.literal: Zhao Yi's measurement of the foot and weight—seven years before it was settled.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao Yi's standard foot-measure and scale required seven years before a decision was reached.

sentences.zh: 公孫濟迂誕醫方，費逾巨萬；

translations.literal: Gongsun Ji's abstruse and extravagant medical formulas cost more than a great myriad;
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Ji's obscure and far-fetched medical prescriptions cost more than ten thousand;

sentences.zh: 徐道慶回互子午，糜耗飲食。

translations.literal: Xu Daoqing's circuitous calendrical adjustments wasted food and drink.
translations.idiomatic: Xu Daoqing's convoluted calendrical revisions wasted vast amounts of grain.

sentences.zh: 常明破律，多曆歲時；

translations.literal: Chang Ming's breaking of laws dragged on through many years;
translations.idiomatic: Chang Ming's violations of statute dragged on for years;

sentences.zh: 王渥亂名，曾無紀極。

translations.literal: Wang Wo's disordering of names knew no limit.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Wo's reckless renaming knew no bounds.

sentences.zh: 張山居未知星位，前已蹂藉太常；

translations.literal: Zhang Shanju, not knowing star positions, had already trampled upon the Chamberlain of Ceremonies;
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Shanju, ignorant of the stars, had already trampled the office of the Grand Master of Ceremonies;

sentences.zh: 曹魏祖不識北辰，今復轔轢太史。

translations.literal: Cao Weizu, not recognizing the North Star, now again crushes the Grand Astrologer.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Weizu, who could not even identify the North Star, now crushes the office of the Grand Astrologer as well.

sentences.zh: 莫不用其短見，便自誇毗，邀射名譽，厚相誣罔。

translations.literal: All of them employ their shallow views, then at once boast and fawn, seek to shoot for reputation, and heavily deceive one another.
translations.idiomatic: All employ their shallow insights, then boast and flatter, chase after renown, and grossly deceive one another.

sentences.zh: 請今日已後，有如此者，若其言不驗，必加重罰，庶令有所畏忌，不敢輕奏狂簡。

translations.literal: I request that from today onward, when there are such persons, if their words are not verified, heavy punishment must be added, so that they may have something to fear and dare not lightly submit reckless and crude proposals.
translations.idiomatic: I ask that from this day forward, anyone who submits such proposals and fails to deliver on them face heavy punishment, so that men will fear to offer reckless and ill-considered memorials.

sentences.zh: 其餘文多不載。

translations.literal: The remaining text is mostly not recorded.
translations.idiomatic: The remainder of the memorial is omitted here for brevity.

sentences.zh: 時蘇威權兼數司，先嘗隱武功，故妥言自負傅岩、滋水之氣，以此激上。

translations.literal: At that time Su Wei wielded authority over several departments; he had earlier concealed his origin from Wugong, and so Tuo spoke of assuming the aura of Fu Yan and Zishui, thereby to provoke the emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Su Wei at the time held authority across several departments; he had once concealed his origins in Wugong, and Tuo's allusion to Fu Yan and Zishui was meant to rouse the emperor's suspicions.

sentences.zh: 書奏，威大銜之。

translations.literal: When the memorial was submitted, Wei nursed great resentment.
translations.idiomatic: When the memorial reached the throne, Su Wei harbored deep resentment.

sentences.zh: 十二年，威定考文學，又與妥更相訶詆。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year, when Wei fixed the examination of literary studies, he and Tuo again mutually reviled each other.
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth year, when Su Wei conducted the literary examination, he and Tuo traded insults once again.

sentences.zh: 威勃然曰：「無何妥，不慮無博士！」

translations.literal: Wei burst out: "Without He Tuo, I need not worry about lacking an erudite!
translations.idiomatic: Su Wei flared up: "Without He Tuo, I hardly need worry about finding an erudite!

sentences.zh: 妥應聲曰：「無蘇威，亦何憂無執事！」

translations.literal: Tuo answered at once: "Without Su Wei, why worry about lacking an office-holder!"
translations.idiomatic: Tuo shot back: "Without Su Wei, why worry about lacking someone to run affairs!"

sentences.zh: 由是與威有隙。

translations.literal: From this he and Wei had a rift.
translations.idiomatic: From that point he and Su Wei were at odds.

sentences.zh: 其後上令妥考定鐘律，妥又上表曰：

translations.literal: Thereafter the emperor ordered Tuo to examine and fix bells and pitch standards, and Tuo again submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: Later the emperor ordered Tuo to examine and fix the bells and pitch pipes, and Tuo submitted another memorial:

sentences.zh: 臣聞明則有禮樂，幽則有鬼神，然則動天地，感鬼神，莫近于禮樂。

translations.literal: I have heard that where there is brightness there are rites and music, and where there is darkness there are ghosts and spirits; thus to move Heaven and earth and touch ghosts and spirits, nothing comes closer than rites and music.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard that where civilization shines, rites and music flourish; in the hidden depths dwell spirits and ghosts—and nothing moves Heaven and earth or touches the spirit world more powerfully than rites and music.

sentences.zh: 又云樂至則無怨，禮至則不爭，揖讓而治天下者，禮樂之謂也。

translations.literal: It is also said that when music reaches its fullness there is no resentment, when rites reach their fullness there is no strife; governing all under Heaven through bowing and yielding—this is what is meant by rites and music.
translations.idiomatic: It is also said that when music is perfected, resentment fades; when rites are perfected, contention ceases. To govern the realm through courtesy and deference—that is the power of rites and music.

sentences.zh: 臣聞樂有二，一曰奸聲，二曰正聲。

translations.literal: I have heard that music has two kinds: first, licentious sounds; second, correct sounds.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard that music divides into two kinds: licentious sounds and correct sounds.

sentences.zh: 夫奸聲感人而逆氣應之，逆氣成象而淫樂興焉。

translations.literal: Licentious sounds move people and perverse qi responds; perverse qi forms images and debauched music arises therefrom.
translations.idiomatic: Licentious sounds move the human heart and perverse vital forces respond; those forces take form and decadent music rises from them.

sentences.zh: 正聲感人而順氣應之，順氣成象而和樂興焉。

translations.literal: Correct sounds move people and harmonious qi responds; harmonious qi forms images and harmonious music arises therefrom.
translations.idiomatic: Correct sounds move the human heart and harmonious vital forces respond; those forces take form and proper music rises from them.

sentences.zh: 故樂行而倫清，耳目聰明，血氣和平，移風易俗，天下皆寧。

translations.literal: Therefore when music is practiced, human relations are clarified, ears and eyes are keen, blood and breath are harmonious, customs are transformed, and all under Heaven is tranquil.
translations.idiomatic: When proper music prevails, human relations are clarified, the senses grow keen, the body's vital forces find balance, customs improve, and all under Heaven lives in peace.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「放鄭聲，遠佞人。」

translations.literal: Confucius said: "Banish the sounds of Zheng; keep petty men at a distance.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said: "Banish the music of Zheng and keep flatterers at a distance.

sentences.zh: 故鄭、衛、宋、趙之聲出，內則發疾，外則傷人。

translations.literal: Therefore when the sounds of Zheng, Wei, Song, and Zhao emerge, inwardly they bring forth illness, outwardly they harm people.
translations.idiomatic: When the music of Zheng, Wei, Song, and Zhao spreads, it breeds illness within and harm without.

sentences.zh: 是以宮亂則荒，其君驕；

translations.literal: Therefore when the gong mode is disordered, there is desolation and the ruler grows arrogant;
translations.idiomatic: When the gong mode falls into disorder, the realm grows wasteful and the ruler arrogant;

sentences.zh: 商亂則陂，其官壞；

translations.literal: When the shang mode is disordered, there is decadence and officials are ruined;
translations.idiomatic: when the shang mode falls into disorder, government grows corrupt and offices collapse;

sentences.zh: 角亂則憂，其人怨；

translations.literal: When the jue mode is disordered, there is sorrow and the people resent;
translations.idiomatic: when the jue mode falls into disorder, grief spreads and the people grow resentful;

sentences.zh: 徵亂則哀，其事勤；

translations.literal: When the zhi mode is disordered, there is grief and affairs are laborious;
translations.idiomatic: when the zhi mode falls into disorder, mourning prevails and affairs grow burdensome;

sentences.zh: 羽亂則危，其財匱。

translations.literal: When the yu mode is disordered, there is peril and wealth is exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: when the yu mode falls into disorder, danger mounts and coffers run dry.

sentences.zh: 五者皆亂，則國亡無日矣。

translations.literal: When all five are disordered, the state's extinction will come within days.
translations.idiomatic: When all five modes fall into disorder together, the state's downfall is imminent.

sentences.zh: 魏文侯問子夏曰：「吾端冕而聽古樂則欲寐，聽鄭、衛之音而不知倦，何也？」

translations.literal: Marquis Wen of Wei asked Zixia: "When I wear full dress and listen to ancient music I wish to sleep; when I listen to the sounds of Zheng and Wei I know no weariness—why is this?
translations.idiomatic: Marquis Wen of Wei asked Zixia: "When I attend in full ceremonial dress to ancient music, I grow drowsy; when I listen to the music of Zheng and Wei, I never grow tired—why?

sentences.zh: 子夏對曰：「夫古樂者，始奏以文，復亂以武，修身及家，平均天下。

translations.literal: Zixia replied: "Ancient music begins its performance with civil refinement and returns to disorder with martial vigor—it cultivates the person and extends to the family, and brings equity to all under Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Zixia answered: "Ancient music opens with civil refinement and closes with martial vigor—it cultivates the self, extends to the family, and brings balance to the realm.

sentences.zh: 鄭、衛之音者，奸聲以亂，溺而不止，颻雜子女，不知父子。

translations.literal: The sounds of Zheng and Wei are licentious sounds used for disorder—drowning without cease, mixing men and women in confusion, not knowing father from son.
translations.idiomatic: The music of Zheng and Wei is licentious sound bred for chaos—an intoxication that never ends, tangling men and women together until father and son are scarcely distinguishable.

sentences.zh: 今君所問者樂也，所愛者音也。

translations.literal: Today what my lord asks about is music, but what my lord loves is mere sound.
translations.idiomatic: What you ask about is music, my lord—but what you love is mere sound.

sentences.zh: 夫樂與音，相近而不同，為人君者，謹審其好惡。」

translations.literal: Music and sound are close yet not the same; for one who serves as ruler, carefully examine likes and dislikes."
translations.idiomatic: Music and mere sound are close kin yet not the same; a ruler must carefully discern what he favors and what he rejects."

sentences.zh: 案聖人之作樂也，非止苟悅耳目而已矣。

translations.literal: Examining the sages' creation of music, it was not merely to gratify the ears and eyes perfunctorily.
translations.idiomatic: Consider how the sages made music: it was never meant merely to tickle the ears and eyes.

sentences.zh: 欲使在宗廟之內，君臣同聽之則莫不和敬；

translations.literal: They intended that within the ancestral temple, when ruler and ministers listened together, none would fail to harmonize in respect;
translations.idiomatic: They meant that in the ancestral temple, when ruler and ministers heard it together, all would be bound in mutual reverence;

sentences.zh: 在鄉里之內，長幼同聽之則莫不和順；

translations.literal: within the village community, when elders and juniors listened together, none would fail to harmonize in concord;
translations.idiomatic: in the village, when old and young heard it together, all would live in easy harmony;

sentences.zh: 在閨門之內，父子同聽之則莫不和親。

translations.literal: within the inner chambers, when father and son listened together, none would fail to harmonize in affection.
translations.idiomatic: within the household, when father and son heard it together, affection would bind them as one.

sentences.zh: 此先王立樂之方也。

translations.literal: This was the method by which the former kings established music.
translations.idiomatic: Such was the way the ancient kings established music.

sentences.zh: 故知聲而不知音者，禽獸是也，知音而不知樂者，眾庶是也。

translations.literal: Thus those who know sound but not tone are like beasts; those who know tone but not music are the common multitude.
translations.idiomatic: Those who perceive sound but not musical tone are no better than beasts; those who grasp tone but not music are the common crowd.

sentences.zh: 故黃鐘大呂，弦歌干戚，僮子皆能儛之。

translations.literal: Thus with the yellow bell and great lü, string songs and shield-axes, even children can dance to them.
translations.idiomatic: Even children can dance to the yellow bell and great lü, to string songs and shield-and-axe dances.

sentences.zh: 能知樂者，其唯君子！

translations.literal: Only the gentleman can truly know music!
translations.idiomatic: Only the gentleman truly understands music!

sentences.zh: 不知聲者，不可與言音，不知音者，不可與言樂，知樂則幾於道矣。

translations.literal: One who does not know sound cannot be spoken to about tone; one who does not know tone cannot be spoken to about music; to know music is to approach the Way.
translations.idiomatic: Speak of tone to one who knows no sound and you waste your breath; speak of music to one who knows no tone and you waste your breath—but to know music is to stand near the Way itself.

sentences.zh: 紂為無道，太師抱樂器以奔周。

translations.literal: When Zhou practiced the Way of perdition, the Grand Music Master fled to Zhou carrying the ritual instruments.
translations.idiomatic: When King Zhou abandoned the Way, the Grand Music Master fled to the Zhou court with the ritual instruments in his arms.

sentences.zh: 晉君德薄，師曠固惜清徵。

translations.literal: The Duke of Jin's virtue was thin, and Music Master Kuang steadfastly withheld the clear zhi mode.
translations.idiomatic: The Duke of Jin's virtue ran thin, and Music Master Kuang steadfastly refused to release the pure zhi mode.

sentences.zh: 上古之時，未有音樂，鼓腹擊壤，樂在其間。

translations.literal: In high antiquity there was as yet no formal music; people patted their bellies and beat the ground—joy lay therein.
translations.idiomatic: In earliest times there was no formal music at all—people simply patted full bellies and beat the earth, and happiness lived in that.

sentences.zh: 《易》曰：「先王作樂崇德，殷薦之上帝，以配祖考。」

translations.literal: The Book of Changes says: "The former kings made music to exalt virtue; in the fullness of their offerings they presented it to the Supreme Lord, to accompany the ancestral fathers."
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Changes says: "The ancient kings made music to magnify virtue, and in the fullness of their rites offered it to the Supreme Lord to honor their ancestors.

sentences.zh: 至於黃帝作《咸池》，顓頊作《六莖》，帝嚳作《五英》，堯作《大章》，舜作《大韶》，禹作《大夏》，湯作《大濩》，武王作《大武》，從夏以來，年代久遠，唯有名字，其聲不可得聞。

translations.literal: As for the Yellow Emperor composing "Xianchi," Zhuanxu composing "Liujing," Emperor Ku composing "Wuying," Yao composing "Dazhang," Shun composing "Dashao," Yu composing "Daxia," Tang composing "Dahu," and King Wu composing "Dawu"—from Xia onward ages have grown remote; only the names remain, and their sounds cannot be heard.
translations.idiomatic: The Yellow Emperor composed "Xianchi," Zhuanxu "Liujing," Emperor Ku "Wuying," Yao "Dazhang," Shun "Dashao," Yu "Daxia," Tang "Dahu," and King Wu "Dawu"—but from Xia onward the ages have grown so distant that only the titles survive; their music can no longer be heard.

sentences.zh: 自殷至周，備於《詩》《頌》。

translations.literal: From Yin through Zhou, music was fully preserved in the Odes and Hymns.
translations.idiomatic: From the Yin through the Zhou, music was fully preserved in the Odes and Hymns.

sentences.zh: 故自聖賢已下，多習樂者，至如伏羲減瑟，文王足琴，仲尼擊磬，子路鼓瑟，漢高擊築，元帝吹簫。

translations.literal: Thus from sages and worthies downward, many studied music—Fuxi reduced the se's strings, King Wen added strings to the qin, Confucius struck the chime-stones, Zilu played the se, Gaozu of Han beat the zhu, and Emperor Yuan played the xiao.
translations.idiomatic: From sages and worthies downward, many mastered music: Fuxi reduced the se's strings, King Wen added strings to the qin, Confucius struck the chime-stones, Zilu played the se, Gaozu of Han beat the zhu, and Emperor Yuan played the xiao.

sentences.zh: 漢高祖之初，叔孫通因秦樂人制宗廟之樂。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Emperor Gaozu of Han, Shusun Tong, drawing on Qin musicians, devised the ancestral temple music.
translations.idiomatic: In the early years of Emperor Gaozu of Han, Shusun Tong drew on Qin court musicians to compose the ancestral temple music.

sentences.zh: 迎神於廟門，奏《嘉至》之樂，猶古降神之樂也。

translations.literal: At the temple gate to welcome the spirits, they performed "Jiazhi" music, like the ancient music for descending spirits.
translations.idiomatic: At the temple gate, to welcome the spirits, they played "Jiazhi"—the modern counterpart of the ancient music for the descent of the spirits.

sentences.zh: 皇帝入廟門，奏《永至》之樂，以為行步之節，猶古《采薺》、《肆夏》也。

translations.literal: When the emperor entered the temple gate, they performed "Yongzhi" music as the measure for his pacing, like the ancient "Caixi" and "Sixia."
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor entered the temple gate, they played "Yongzhi" to mark the pace of his steps—the counterpart of the ancient "Caixi" and "Sixia."

sentences.zh: 乾豆上薦，奏《登歌》之樂，猶古清廟之歌也。

translations.literal: When dried meats and beans were offered, they performed "Dengge" music, like the ancient hymn of the Pure Temple.
translations.idiomatic: When dried meats and beans were presented, they sang "Dengge"—the counterpart of the ancient hymn of the Pure Temple.

sentences.zh: 《登歌》再終，奏《休成》之樂，美神饗也。

translations.literal: When "Dengge" had been performed twice, they played "Xiucheng" music, praising the spirits' partaking.
translations.idiomatic: After "Dengge" had been sung twice, they played "Xiucheng" to celebrate the spirits' acceptance of the offering.

sentences.zh: 皇帝就東廂坐定，奏《永安》之樂，美禮成也。

translations.literal: When the emperor took his seat in the east wing, they played "Yong'an" music, praising the completion of the rite.
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor took his seat in the east wing, they played "Yong'an" to celebrate the rite's completion.

sentences.zh: 其《休成》、《永至》二曲，叔孫通所制也。

translations.literal: The two pieces "Xiucheng" and "Yongzhi" were composed by Shusun Tong.
translations.idiomatic: The two pieces "Xiucheng" and "Yongzhi" were Shusun Tong's own compositions.

sentences.zh: 漢高祖廟奏《武德》、《文始》、《五行》之儛，當春秋時，陳公子完奔齊，陳是舜後，故齊有《韶》樂，孔子在齊聞《韶》，三月不知肉味是也。

translations.literal: At Gaozu's temple they performed the dances "Wude," "Wenshi," and "Wuxing." In Spring and Autumn times, Prince Wan of Chen fled to Qi; Chen was descended from Shun, hence Qi had the "Shao" music—this is why Confucius, hearing "Shao" in Qi, forgot the taste of meat for three months.
translations.idiomatic: At Gaozu's temple they danced "Wude," "Wenshi," and "Wuxing." In Spring and Autumn times Prince Wan of Chen fled to Qi; as Chen was descended from Shun, Qi preserved the "Shao" music—when Confucius heard it in Qi and forgot the taste of meat for three months, it was this music he heard.

sentences.zh: 秦始皇滅齊，得齊《韶》樂。

translations.literal: When the First Emperor of Qin destroyed Qi, he obtained Qi's "Shao" music.
translations.idiomatic: When the First Emperor of Qin conquered Qi, he seized Qi's "Shao" music.

sentences.zh: 漢高祖滅秦，《韶》傳于漢，高祖改名《文始》，以示不相襲也。

translations.literal: When Gaozu destroyed Qin, "Shao" passed to Han; Gaozu renamed it "Wenshi" to show he did not simply inherit the former dynasty.
translations.idiomatic: When Gaozu overthrew Qin, "Shao" passed to Han; he renamed it "Wenshi" to show he was not merely inheriting the old order.

sentences.zh: 《五行儛》者，本周《大武》樂也，始皇改曰《五行》。

translations.literal: The "Wuxing Dance" was originally Zhou's "Dawu" music; the First Emperor renamed it "Wuxing."
translations.idiomatic: The "Wuxing Dance" was originally Zhou's "Dawu" music; the First Emperor retitled it "Wuxing."

sentences.zh: 及于孝文，復作四時之儛，以示天下安和，四時順也。

translations.literal: Under Emperor Wen, the dances of the four seasons were restored, to show the realm was at peace and the seasons in order.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Wen the dances of the four seasons were restored, proclaiming that the realm was at peace and the seasons ran true.
